tagline: Follow the Mississippi from Twain’s Hannibal to French houses and earthquake country.
intro: Missouri’s Great River Road follows a Mississippi corridor of river towns, St. Louis city life and French heritage at Ste. Genevieve. The Mississippi River Parkway Commission presents the drive through its cultural variety, from Mark Twain’s Hannibal to the St. Louis Arch and the earthquake history of New Madrid.

At the corridor’s southern end, a concrete arch records an earlier road improvement. The Mississippi County, Arkansas Road Improvement District erected it in 1924 after paving the North–South Road, already a major route between St. Louis and Memphis. That arch now crosses U.S. 61 at the Missouri–Arkansas line, with a different state greeting on each side.

Travel south from Canton through Hannibal and Louisiana toward St. Charles and St. Louis. Beyond the city come Ste. Genevieve and Cape Girardeau. At Cape Girardeau, the downtown floodwall carries a 24-panel mural, with Riverfront Park and views of the Mississippi behind it. Continue south to New Madrid. At the southern end, U.S. 61 passes Holland and continues to Blytheville, Arkansas.

moments.title: Hannibal
moments.text: Hannibal supplied Mark Twain with childhood settings for The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. Mark Twain Cave inspired the episode in which Tom and Becky become lost. The town also commemorated its writer with a lighthouse, built in 1933 as a public works project under Franklin D. Roosevelt. Roosevelt, John F. Kennedy and Bill Clinton each lit it on ceremonial occasions. For a view of the landscape behind the fiction, Lover’s Leap overlooks both downtown Hannibal and the Mississippi River. The Mark Twain Boyhood Home & Museum marked its centennial in 2012.

moments.title: Ste. Genevieve
moments.text: The flood of 1785 sent Ste. Genevieve to a new location two miles north and about half a mile inland. Louis Bolduc salvaged parts of his damaged riverfront house and incorporated them into a larger house built in 1792–1793. Among the town’s oldest surviving buildings are houses with upright wooden posts, either planted in the earth or set on a raised foundation. In the posts-in-the-ground houses, separate stone pillars support the floor. Three of the nation’s five surviving examples stand in Ste. Genevieve. Posts set partly in dirt left these walls vulnerable to floods, termites and rot, even as stone pillars carried the floors.

moments.title: New Madrid
moments.text: New Madrid sits on the north side of Kentucky Bend, where the Mississippi makes an oxbow around a piece of Kentucky. The sequence began in December 1811, followed by further major earthquakes in January and February 1812. On February 7, 1812, an earthquake destroyed the town. Uplift along the Reelfoot Fault produced temporary waterfalls at the bend and waves that traveled upstream. Across the region, the earthquakes collapsed riverbanks, destroyed sandbars and made some islands disappear. The New Madrid Historical Museum interprets the southern Missouri earthquakes of 1811 and 1812.
